Healthcare stocks fell again on Wednesday after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) proposed a new rule that would toughen oversight of Medicare, Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), and the health insurance marketplace. Sagging shares of managed care providers weighed on the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI). UnitedHealth Group stock (UNH), one of the Dow's largest components with a 4.32% weighting, fell by more than 10%. Humana (HUM) dropped 13%. Cigna (CI) shares declined by 3%. CVS Health (CVS), which is in the process of splitting up its retail and insurance businesses, fell 5%. Read more: Medicare out-of-pocket costs are rising in 2027 The rule, called the Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare, or CRUSH, would increase audits of insurance providers and allow CMS to recover improper payments. It would also require providers to report changes to enrollment information within 30 days, among other conditions. In the release shared on Monday, officials pointed to bad actors billing Medicare for nonexistent wheelchairs, enrolling healthy seniors in Medicare-funded hospice care, and signing people up for Marketplace plans without their consent as examples of the kinds of fraud this rule aims to crack down on. CMS said the rule could save taxpayers nearly $90 billion over the next 10 years. The proposal is open to public comment until Jan. 19, 2027. However, Oppenheimer analysts said they expect the proposal to face similar legal scrutiny to that of a framework a federal court struck down in 2025. Furthermore, the team noted that the $90 billion cost savings likely reflect CMS recouping repayments rather than broad savings to healthcare programs. "We believe CMS will be subject to the same legal challenges that it faced in 2025," the analysts wrote. "The substantially larger collection estimate reflects broader auditing, with recoveries concentrated in 2028–2030. This is a proposed rule, so CMS could choose to make adjustments in the final rule. Even if the rule were implemented as is, and it were upheld by the courts, we believe plans would incorporate the prospective cost into bids rather than absorb an unchanged recurring earnings burden." title: UnitedHealth Faces $9 Billion Industry Clawback Under New CMS Rules, Sending UNH Stock Below $350 - FXLeaders
content: UnitedHealth Group (NYSE: UNH) stock has fallen back below $350s as proposed Medicare Advantage audit reforms, political pressure to break up healthcare conglomerates and rising medical costs intensify concerns about earnings and margins. UnitedHealth shares have come under renewed selling pressure, falling approximately 9% on Wednesday after failing to consolidate gains above $400. The stock has retreated into the $350s, with investors reassessing the regulatory and operational risks facing the managed-care sector. A major catalyst emerged on November 16, when the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services proposed the Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare, known as the CRUSH rule. The proposal would formalise risk-adjustment data validation audits and allow regulators to extrapolate findings from sampled claims across entire Medicare Advantage contracts. Audits could reach back to payment year 2018, while CMS estimates the framework could recover approximately $9 billion per year across the industry. UnitedHealth faces significant exposure because it operates the country’s largest Medicare Advantage business. Mizuho analyst Ann Hynes identified UnitedHealth and Humana as the insurers most affected by the proposed changes, followed by CVS Health, Elevance Health, Centene and Molina Healthcare. Plitical pressure is adding another challenge. Senator Elizabeth Warren has called for breaking up vertically integrated healthcare conglomerates, specifically naming UnitedHealth, CVS and Cigna and citing the proposed Break Up Big Medicine Act. Restrictions on insurers owning pharmacy benefit managers and healthcare providers could threaten UnitedHealth’s integrated Optum business model, potentially reducing operational flexibility and creating additional regulatory costs. Elevated medical utilisation, particularly in outpatient and specialty services, is also weighing on insurers’ margins. If healthcare costs rise faster than premiums, underwriting profitability could deteriorate further. Although UnitedHealth retains substantial scale and cash-flow generation, regulatory uncertainty and medical-cost pressures leave the stock vulnerable. Investors will watch management guidance and the $350 support area closely as the company faces growing challenges to its earnings outlook.

A sign pointing out the sights and sounds visitors might encounter at College Woods in New Hampshire helped improve their moods, a University of New Hampshire researcher found. “There’s a huge body of evidence saying being in nature is good for us,” said Lauren Ferguson, Ph.D., an assistant professor in the University of New Hampshire’s Department of Recreation Management and Policy. Ferguson conducted research at College Woods in New Hampshire to study how walking outdoors affects people’s feelings. “What I did find is that the perception of biodiversity is more important than the actual biodiversity,” Ferguson said. She found that simply placing a sign at the entrance to College Woods listing the sights and sounds visitors might encounter had a positive effect on their moods. Ferguson said people’s perceptions of their surroundings mattered more than the specific sights they encountered. The sign also made visitors more aware of their surroundings by telling them what to look for, making the experience more restorative. “Our normal day-to-day life is extremely cognitively depleting, but being in a place like this allows your brain to still remain focused and remain engaged while you’re also simultaneously recovering from that fatigue,” Ferguson said. Ferguson said the biggest positive effects were seen during warmer months, but nature walks can improve mood in any season. She encourages people to take walks outdoors, even during colder months. title: Why Is UnitedHealth Stock Falling? - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036? UnitedHealth Group (UNH) stock fell 5.4% on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 1.0%. There was no announcement, earnings report or filing from the company. A market commentary published that day said the shares fell amid renewed regulatory scrutiny. All seven other managed health care companies worth $2 billion or more fell too. Management’s comments on its October earnings call, weeks before the fall, show which parts of UnitedHealth’s business sit closest to regulators. By management’s own account, rules set outside the company affect both its government plans and its commercial business. On its October 13 call, management said policy-driven regulatory developments continue to reshape the industry. In Medicaid, UnitedHealth works with states on rates that reflect the impacts of regulatory actions. Management said the timing of those updates remains uneven. The company expects 2026 to be the low point for core Medicaid margins. It expects those margins to come in moderately better than a 1% loss. In the commercial business, management pointed to the dispute process under the No Surprises Act. It said a small number of clinician groups and third-party organizations abuse that process. Arbitration awards can reach nearly 6% of total medical spend in some regions, management said. UnitedHealth has little room to absorb such costs. The company recorded a net margin of 3.5% over the twelve months to September 2026, down from 4.0% a year earlier. Did UnitedHealth Fall With Other Managed Care Companies? Yes, and it fell further than any of them. All seven other companies worth $2 billion or more in its managed health care sub-industry fell on Tuesday, logging a median drop of 3.9%. Just one of them fell 5% or more: Molina Healthcare, down 5.1%. Every company on UnitedHealth’s peer list fell as well, among them Humana, down 3.9%. The broader health care sector fell less, with the sector fund XLV down 1.4%. UnitedHealth moved with its group, and its drop was larger than the group’s median. A fall this large is rare for UnitedHealth. Only one other session in the prior year brought a fall at least this big: a 19.6% drop on January 27, 2026. Over the past twelve months, the stock returned 24.3%, against 10.3% for the S&P 500. Shares climbed from a 52-week closing low of $259.02 on March 27 to a high of $436.35 on July 21. Tuesday’s close of $389.68 left the stock below that high. UnitedHealth trades at 0.78 times its sales over the past twelve months, against 3.2 times for the S&P 500. UnitedHealth is expected to report its fourth-quarter 2026 results in January 2027. The number to watch is the medical care ratio, the share of premiums spent on care, which the company put at 88.4% for the third quarter. Tuesday showed how one stock can drop with its whole group on a day its company announced nothing. Holding on is easier when your portfolio falls less than the market. A major milestone in space exploration is happening Wednesday morning as NASA's Voyager 1 will reach the distance of one light day from Earth. A light day is a measure of how far light moves in 24 hours. At a speed of 186,000 miles per second, one light day is 16 billion miles. One light day is the farthest away any object made by humanity has ever traveled from Earth. Voyager 1 launched in 1977 with a team that included a University of New Hampshire scientist. News 9 spoke to the late Dr. William Webber in 1989. He said even then, NASA never expected Voyager to last that long. "When we were designing this instrument and planning it in the early 70s, we never dreamed that it would last more than a few years," Webber said. "This instrument's operated for 15 years perfectly. title: In Full Swing: Polka Party Radio Show Still Going Strong After Nearly 40 Years - University of New Hampshire
content: Gary Sredzienski ’85, host of WUNH's Polka Party show. (Photo credit: Martha Ladd) When WUNH was exploring potential alternative music programming to add to its airwaves in 1987, Gary Sredzienski ’85 hopped in his car, drove back home to Connecticut, grabbed about 10 polka records from his father’s collection, and essentially as a gag, launched the Polka Party show. Nearly four decades later, the party still hasn’t ended. Polka Party will celebrate its 40th year on air next July, and it remains one of WUNH’s most beloved shows, with an audience that is as strong and engaged as ever. Sredzienski receives numerous emails and letters from avid listeners sharing their personal stories, and he spends days meticulously scripting each Saturday’s show. What began on a whim has become something of an unexpected career. “It started as pretty much a joke. But then the letters started coming in, and I just couldn’t quit,” Sredzienski says. “It changed the trajectory of my life, big-time.” That isn’t an exaggeration. Sredzienski was working for the U.S. Forest Service when the show began, but that career lasted only five years, as the notoriety the show provided allowed him to quit that gig and start playing accordion full time – which he’s been doing since 1990. The show has certainly evolved over the years. Though the title has stayed the same, Polka Party features a wide variety of ethnic music, from its origins in Polish American tunes to old American, Polish village, Russian, Jewish, and Scandinavian music, among other varieties. The show may be a labor of love, but it does indeed require some labor. Because Sredzienski includes a lot of narration and storytelling, he scripts out the entire show every week – 40 pages of handwritten notes. He typically begins the process on Wednesday for each Saturday morning episode (the show airs from 9-to-11 a.m. every week). Sredzienski says he thinks the show first gained traction because it tapped into nostalgia from the radio days of the 1940s, 50s and 60s, when ethnic stations were extremely popular in communities throughout the U.S. To maintain some of that nostalgic flair, everything Sredzienski plays is on records – he brings a bag of 50 or 60 of his own to the studio every weekend. Despite the old-world touches that connect so strongly with his audience, modern advancements have taken the show to a new level – and to new listeners. When he first began broadcasting, WUNH could only reach about a 60-mile radius, Sredzienski says. But because the show is now accessible on the internet, he’s heard from listeners tuning in from a variety of far-flung locales. “I’ve heard from people who tune in from Istanbul every week, and one guy reached out and said he was at a bar in Romania and told people he knew me, and he got a bunch of free drinks,” Sredzienski says. “Since we’ve been on the internet, it’s just opened things up incredibly. It’s a different ballgame now.” Polka Party is putting that expanded reach to good use this week as part of the WUNH marathon, the station’s signature annual fundraising event during which a live DJ is on-air 24 hours each day for seven consecutive days. The event is among the most anticipated of the year at the station and routinely brings in the largest sum of fundraising support to WUNH during any one stretch of time throughout the year (you can donate here.) “Only one Polka Party show a year do I ask listeners to call in their support,” Sredzienski says. “Of course the university provides some funding, but we also rely on donations from the listeners because running a radio station is an expensive endeavor.” Polka Party has opened doors as a musician for Sredzienski that he would never have imagined possible. His music has been featured in six movies, he’s played at the Smithsonian and the Kennedy Center, and he’s been invited to a number of international locales. Marathon week at WUNH is underway! Give now to support UNH's student-run radio station, which has been operating for 65 strong years. Marathon Week is WUNH's signature annual fundraising event, featuring a live DJ on air 24 hours each day throughout the week and marathon-specific specialty shows. Listeners and supporters can donate any amount to claim "out of this world" swag including: Don’t miss your chance to be part of this memorable week and to help keep the station thriving. Give any amount now! “It’s given me the most beautiful life,” Sredzienski says. That’s why he’s continued to broadcast for almost 40 years – he views the show “as a community service,” a way to provide both a thank you and a positive outlet to the fans that changed the course of his life and career. Though many of his original listeners have passed away, he still hears from people who say their children grew up listening to the show. One woman told him the show “makes me a better person.” It’s that sense of joy and positivity that remains at the heart of Polka Party, which has survived decades of change in the music and entertainment industry and still serves its original purpose. “I want to make it an oasis for people so they can just get away from the reality of today and be in this time capsule. It’s like listening to something vintage out of the past,” Sredzienski says. “It’s an escape. I want it to be an escape for people. I want to welcome everybody, because that’s the point of radio – you don’t want to shut people out, you want to welcome as many people as you can.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. NORTH HAVEN, Conn. (WFSB) - State police have charged a 31-year-old man with manslaughter and other counts in an Oct. 16 wrong-way crash on Interstate 91 that killed University of New Haven student, 21-year-old Ryan O’Shea. Troopers charged Guillermo Carmona-Lopez after obtaining an arrest warrant, police said. He was arrested Nov. 9 and arraigned from a hospital bed. Troopers responded to I-91 southbound near Exit 9 in North Haven for a report of a wrong-way crash, state police said. A preliminary investigation found O’Shea was driving a Honda Accord south in the left lane. Carmona-Lopez was driving a Chevrolet Silverado north in the southbound lanes and hit the Accord head-on, according to police. The Accord went into the left-center lane, where a Jeep Grand Cherokee hit it, police said. The Accord then went into the right lane and onto the right shoulder, where a GMC Terrain hit it. O’Shea was pronounced dead at the scene. Carmona-Lopez was taken to Yale New Haven Hospital with serious, life-threatening injuries, police said. The other drivers were hospitalized with minor injuries. State police said Carmona-Lopez’s license was suspended. One witness told police that as they neared the Exit 8 off-ramp, he saw headlights coming toward them. The witness said there was a car in the left lane approaching them, according to the account police recorded. Another witness captured the collision on a dash camera. Police said the video shows Carmona-Lopez’s truck drove toward and passed at least 18 vehicles before it struck O’Shea’s car. A trooper at the scene said Carmona-Lopez could not explain what happened and smelled of alcohol. Carmona-Lopez allegedly told police in an interview at the hospital that he drank four beers starting around 8 that night. He also said that once he got on the highway, he did not remember anything after that, according to the account police recorded. The arrest warrant states his blood alcohol level was .22 and .21. The legal limit is .08. He was held on $500,000 bond and had a bedside arraignment at the hospital Nov. 12. At last check, he remained in the custody of the state Department of Correction. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said Carmona-Lopez is from Mexico and entered the country illegally. ICE said Border Patrol arrested him in May 2013 after he entered the country illegally. The agency said he was deported, then reentered illegally, which is a felony. ICE said Border Patrol arrested him again and issued a final order of removal. The agency said he got back into the country at an unknown time and place. “Ryan O’Shea was just 21 years old,” said acting ICE Director David J. Venturella. “He was a college student, a hockey player and a young man preparing for a career protecting others. His family should be celebrating his accomplishments and looking forward to his future. Instead, they’re mourning a life tragically cut short. We extend our deepest condolences to Ryan’s family, friends and teammates. His death is a devastating loss, and he deserves to be remembered for the life he lived and the future he was working so hard to build.” O’Shea was a senior at the University of New Haven and an assistant captain on the school’s club hockey team. He was heading home from a game, and he was studying to become a police officer. The university held a remembrance for O’Shea in October and unveiled a plaque with his name on campus. “I think it’s good that they made the arrest, I think it’s necessary and hopefully provide closure to the family and to us on campus here,” said Jack Winzer, a University of New Haven freshman. Police are still investigating the crash. They have not said where they believe Carmona-Lopez got on I-91. He passed a number of cars going the wrong way before the collision. The medical care ratio measures the share of premium revenue an insurer spends on members healthcare. A lower ratio means more of each premium dollar is available for administrative costs and profit. UnitedHealthcare serves tens of millions of people across commercial, Medicare and Medicaid plans, making it one of the largest health insurers in the world. Optum serves an even broader population through pharmacy benefit management, care delivery and health data services. title: What is the Climate Action Clinic at UNH and is it right for you? - University of New Hampshire
content: If you're interested in sustainability but aren't sure how to turn it into real-world experience, the Climate Action Clinic at the University of New Hampshire is worth exploring. Open to students of any major, this course puts you to work alongside actual businesses, nonprofits, and communities to help them understand and reduce their carbon footprints. Here's what the Clinic is, what you'll do, and what makes it different from a typical college course. The Climate Action Clinic is a semester-long, two-credit course offered through UNH's Sustainability Institute and Peter T. Paul College of Business and Economics. Students work in small teams to complete a carbon footprint analysis for a real organization, using a professional-grade online platform called SIMAP (Sustainability Indicator Management and Analysis Platform), which is hosted by UNH and used by hundreds of colleges and universities across the country. What is a carbon footprint analysis, and why does it matter? A carbon footprint analysis, also called a greenhouse gas inventory, helps an organization understand how much greenhouse gas pollution it produces, and which activities are driving that pollution. It’s what allows organizations to identify practical, cost-effective ways to reduce their emissions. Carbon accounting is an increasingly marketable professional skill and the Climate Action Clinic is designed to give you a working foundation. Do you need to be a sustainability-related major to participate? No, the Clinic is for all majors. Your team will be from different majors, which strengthens the quality of the analysis and reflects how sustainability work happens in professional settings. For Cole Fuller '24, '26G, who majored in analytical economics, the Clinic connected dots he hadn't expected. "The Clinic was really valuable for me to recognize the connection between my skillset, which was more data/math focused, and my interest in sustainability. As an analytical econ major, I wasn't aware of how much opportunity there would be for me in the field." What’s it like to be in the Clinic and how is it different from a typical course? Students tour a Climate Action Clinic client's facility. You'll apply sustainability concepts to a real problem for a real client, within a real deadline. In the first few weeks, students are introduced to the basics of carbon accounting and are matched with a client organization, which could be a business, nonprofit, or municipality – the range of industries students work with is broad. Teams spend the bulk of the semester working through their client's carbon data, verifying a baseline carbon footprint, and analyzing potential meaningful steps toward emissions reduction goals. The semester wraps up with teams presenting their completed work to clients. A peer mentor, a student who has completed the Clinic at least once, serves as your team leader to help guide and support the whole team. This structure means you're supported throughout the process, even if you come in with no prior experience. It also means there's a path to grow within the Clinic itself. Durga Raja '25, an environmental resource economics and sustainability dual major who is now a consultant at Eversource, started as a student team member in her sophomore year and returned as a peer mentor for five additional semesters. "That experience showed me how sustainability goals can look very different across sectors, while giving me the chance to collaborate with peers, work directly with clients, and make a real impact." Students present data and findings to their Climate Action Clinic client. You’ll develop a working understanding of greenhouse gas accounting standards and carbon neutrality claims, and experience applying those concepts. Beyond the technical skills, you will build consulting experience, practice communicating complex information to non-specialist audiences, and develop team-based project management skills. For some students, the Clinic also clarifies a career direction they hadn't previously considered. Cole Fuller returned to take the Clinic a second time as a peer mentor, went on to complete an AmeriCorps service term focused on residential energy efficiency, earned a master's degree in economics, and is now UNH's Energy Systems Analyst. "The Clinic inspired me to pursue jobs that were more sustainability focused.” If you want hands-on sustainability experience, are curious about carbon or environmental reporting as a career direction, or simply want to contribute to something with real-world impact while earning credit, the Clinic is for you. Because it is open to all majors, it is also a way to explore sustainability work without committing to a full program change. As Cole Fuller's path shows, the skills developed in the Clinic can translate across industries and career directions well beyond what you might initially anticipate. If the Climate Action Clinic sounds like a fit for you, take these next steps: The Climate Action Clinic is offered each spring semester. Check the Clinic website for course pre-registration before spring course registration opens each fall. Explore UNH's sustainability dual major, which can be paired with any primary major and for which the Clinic counts as an elective credit.
